sections.title_en: The Mitzvot of Orla and Neta Revai
sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva not to derive benefit from orla fruit, which is the fruit growing in the first three years of a tree, and it is a mitzva to bring the fruit growing in the fourth year up to Jerusalem and to eat it in holiness and in praise of God, and through this blessing will be drawn to the fruit that will grow from the fifth year onward. As it is stated (Vayikra 19:23-25): "And when you come into the land and plant any tree for food, you shall treat its fruit as forbidden (lit. 'uncircumcised'); three years it shall be forbidden to you, it shall not be eaten. And in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy, for giving praise to the Lord. And in the fifth year you may eat its fruit, so that it may increase its yield for you; I am the Lord your God."

'Orla' means being sealed. Therefore, one of 'uncircumcised heart' (Yeḥezkel 44:9) is one whose heart is sealed; one of 'uncircumcised ears' (Yirmiyahu 6:10) is one whose ears are sealed from hearing; and one of 'uncircumcised lips' (Shemot 6:12) is a person whose lips are sealed from speaking. Thus we were commanded that the fruit of the first three years be sealed off to us, that we not eat it and not derive benefit from it (Rashi and Rashbam, Vayikra there).

On the day the Children of Israel crossed the Jordan in the days of Yehoshua bin Nun and entered the Land, they became obligated in the mitzva of orla, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:23): "And when you come into the land and plant." And even a tree that a gentile planted in his field from then on is obligated in orla and its fruit is forbidden to us for benefit, as it is stated (there): "any tree for food" – to include a tree that a gentile planted (Torat Kohanim there).

Outside the Land, the law of orla applies as a 'halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai' (a law transmitted to Moshe at Sinai), and the halakha established that it applies only when there is certainty that the fruit is orla; but whenever there is a doubt about it, even though it is very likely that the fruit is orla, there is no prohibition in it, for doubtful orla in the Land is forbidden, and outside the Land it is permitted (Mishna and Yerushalmi, Orla 3:7; Bavli Kiddushin 39a; SA 294:8; below, section 11). The borders of the Land with regard to the mitzva of orla are the borders of those who came up from Egypt. And even according to those who hold that the southern Arava is outside the border of those who came up from Egypt, since it is under the rule of the State of Israel, the mitzva applies to it by Torah law (below 12:2, n. 2; 17).1

Whether one plants a seed or plants a cutting, from the time they take root in the ground one begins to count three years for them (section 4 will explain how the years are calculated).

[Video]

notes_en.en:
Mishna Orla 1:2: "When our forefathers came to the Land – if they found [a tree already] planted, it was exempt; if they planted, even though they had not conquered [the Land], it was obligated." For it is stated, "And when you come" – immediately when you come (Yerushalmi there). And so it was ruled in the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni Ve-neta Revai 10:9). Some Aḥaronim hold that according to those who hold that the second sanctification, with which the Land was sanctified in the days of the Second Temple, was annulled with its destruction, orla nowadays is rabbinic (Mishneh La-melekh, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 10:11). And some say that only when the majority of Israel dwells in the Land is one obligated in orla by Torah law, as it is stated, "When you come" (Tzlaḥ, Berakhot 36a). In practice, it was ruled that even nowadays the mitzva of orla in the Land is by Torah law (SA YD 294:8; Radbaz, Mabit, Maharashdam, Maharit). However, in a pressing situation one joins the opinion of the lenient authorities as a factor toward permission (Rav Herzog, Pesakim U-khtavim 3:1; Yabi'a Omer 6, YD 24).
Since doubtful orla outside the Land is permitted, the Sages said (Berakhot 36b): "Whoever is lenient in the Land, the halakha follows him outside the Land," and therefore the peel of the caper does not have the law of orla. And the same applies to every dispute regarding orla: wherever there is a Tanna or Amora who is lenient, outside the Land the halakha follows him (see SA 294:17). And it appears that in disputes of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim as well one should lean toward the lenient side; but when the stringent opinion is very compelling, it is proper to be stringent.

sections.body_en:
The reason for the mitzva is to honor God with the first fruits of the tree, to eat them in holiness in Jerusalem and to praise God through them for all the good He has granted us. And since generally the fruits growing in the first three years are not plentiful and choice, it is not fitting to praise God with them, and therefore the Torah forbade them, so that the beginning of our eating will be in holiness and in praise of God in the fourth year, when many good fruits already grow. And through this, the pleasantness of God and His blessing will rest upon the fruits growing in all the years, and eating them will be connected to faith and will grant vitality to add goodness and blessing in the world. Similarly, the Torah commanded to sanctify the firstborn of man and the firstborn of animals and the bikkurim (first fruits). And such is also the reason of the mitzvot of ḥadash, teruma, ḥalla and the first shearing (see Ramban, Vayikra there; Ḥinukh 246-247).

We further learn from this mitzva the value of self-restraint, which is very important and beneficial. The ability to restrain oneself and to defer the satisfaction of desire to the appropriate time is a necessary condition for a person's success in this world and in the World to Come. For example, it is known that a person who studies diligently in his youth will be more successful in his personal life and in his livelihood, and nevertheless many young people do not succeed in restraining themselves, are drawn after their impulses and waste their time on various amusements. Likewise, it is known that dating relationships between young men and women not for the sake of marriage harm their ability to marry and to establish a faithful home with love, and nevertheless many do not succeed in restraining themselves, and are drawn after their impulses into stormy relationships that do not lead to a true covenant. And likewise there are people who do not succeed in restraining themselves from wasting their money on luxuries, such as buying an apartment more expensive than they can afford, and do not succeed in saving money
to help their children acquire a profession and marry, and to support themselves in their old age. Adam, the first man, too, was drawn after his impulse and sinned because he did not restrain himself from eating from the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil, and thereby brought death upon himself and his descendants. Through the mitzva of orla, a person learns to see his fruits growing and to refrain from benefiting from them, and in this way he learns to overcome his impulse and to restrain himself. This is what the Sages said (Vayikra Rabba 25:2): "Who will remove the dust from your eyes, Adam, the first man, for you could not stand by your commandment for a single hour, and behold, your children wait for orla three years" (see Beitza 25b).

The Sages further said that the fruits of the first years express a desire to come into actuality before the proper time, without the appropriate restraint, and therefore they have no completeness and impurity clings to them. The fruits of the first three years correspond to the three evil and hard kelipot (husks), which seal and conceal the light. And the fourth year corresponds to the thin kelipa in which good and evil are mixed, and its fruits are rectified by bringing them up to Jerusalem and eating them in holiness (Zohar vol. 3, 87a; Sha'arei Ora, Gate 5; Pardes Rimonim, Gate 25:7).

[Video]

The fruits growing in the first three years are forbidden to eat and to derive benefit from. Therefore, it is forbidden to light a lamp with oil from orla fruit, and it is forbidden to heat an oven with orla fruit. Likewise, it is forbidden to place orla fruit in the ground for the purpose of fertilizing, but it is permitted to throw them on the ground without intending to fertilize. Even for the sake of a mitzva it is forbidden to use orla fruit; therefore, an etrog of orla is invalid for the four species on Sukkot (Sukka 34b; SA YD 294:24; Peninei Halakha, Sukkot 4:12). Likewise, it is forbidden to benefit from the scent of orla fruit (SA 108:7).2

Likewise, it is forbidden to dye a garment with dye produced from orla fruit. And the garment that was dyed with orla fruit is forbidden for benefit, and so that people will not stumble with it, it must be burned (Yerushalmi Orla 3:1; Bavli Kiddushin 56b). And whenever there is a concern that people will come to benefit from orla fruit, it is a mitzva to burn them or destroy them in another way that will prevent the possibility of benefiting from them. And if possible, it is good to remove the blossoms or the fruits from the tree while they are still small, so that people will not stumble with them.3

Everything that grows with the fruit is forbidden for benefit, including the fruit's seeds and peel, as well as juice that comes out of it. But the tree, its leaves and its blossoms are permitted for benefit. Likewise, the fruit while still very small, to the point that it is not considered a fruit and is called semadar (blossom-stage fruit) – is permitted for benefit. But once it reaches the stage of boser (unripe fruit), even though it is not yet fit for eating, it is already considered a fruit and the prohibition of orla applies to it (Mishna Orla 1:7-9; SA 294:1-2).4

It is forbidden to sow the seeds of orla fruit, and likewise it is forbidden to place an orla fruit in the ground so that a tree will grow from it. But it is permitted to plant a branch of an orla tree, since there is no prohibition of benefit in the tree (Mishna Orla 1:9). If one transgressed and planted an orla fruit, the tree that grows is permitted for benefit, for we hold the rule: "Zeh ve-zeh gorem – mutar" (when both this and that cause it, it is permitted). That is, when there are two causes for the tree's growth – the forbidden fruit and the permitted soil – the tree that grows is permitted for benefit (SA 294:12).

The prohibition of orla also applies to a gentile's tree, whose fruits are forbidden to a Jew for benefit. However, a gentile is permitted to benefit from orla fruit that grew on his own tree or on a Jew's tree, for the prohibition of orla applies to Jews and not to gentiles. But since the fruits are forbidden to a Jew for benefit, a Jew is forbidden to sell his orla fruit to a gentile, and likewise he is forbidden to give them as a gift to a gentile or even to feed them to a wild animal, for in this way too the Jew benefits from them (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 8:16).

However, before the orla fruits have begun to grow, it is permitted to sell them to a gentile, for since the Jew receives the money even before the fruits have come into the world, he does not benefit from the fruits but from the tree, which he is selling, and the tree is permitted for benefit (SA 294:15; Nekudot Ha-kesef there). And this is on condition that there is no concern that the gentile will sell the orla fruit to a Jew and cause him to stumble in a prohibition, for example, where the gentile sells them in a place where there are no Jews.

[Video]

notes_en.en: In the Yerushalmi, Orla 3:1, and the Bavli, Pesaḥim 21b: according to Ḥizkiya, wherever it is stated "it shall not be eaten" (lo ye'akhel), as with orla, it is forbidden for benefit as well, for if they were to permit benefiting from the fruits, people could sell them and buy food with the proceeds, so that through them they would come to eating. And when the prohibition is stated in the language "you shall not eat" (lo tokhlu), as with the prohibition of eating nevela and tereifa, the food is forbidden to eat but permitted for benefit. So too wrote the Rosh (Ḥullin 7:17). And according to Rabbi Abahu, every expression of a prohibition of eating includes benefit as well, except in places where there is another derivation that permits benefit. So too wrote the Rambam (Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 8:15). They further learned from the fact that the expression 'orla' is stated three times that all types of benefit are included (Pesaḥim 22b). (On the permission to throw them on the ground without intending to fertilize, see Tosafot, Avoda Zara 43b, s.v. 'Amru lo', and Mishpetei Eretz 10:9.)

In the Mishna, Temura 33b: "And these are the ones that are burned: ḥametz on Pesaḥ – shall be burned; and impure teruma, and orla, and kilei ha-kerem – those whose way is to be burned shall be burned, and those whose way is to be buried shall be buried." From Tosafot it is implied that it is obligatory to burn kilei ha-kerem and orla, as it is stated (Devarim 22:9): "pen tikdash" (lest it be forfeited) – "pen tukad esh" (lest it be set on fire) (Kiddushin 56b). In contrast, according to the Ritva there is no obligation to burn them; rather, they stand to be burned. And the Responsa Binyan Tziyon 101 explained that this is so that people will not stumble and benefit from them, and therefore what is fit for burial is buried; thus there is no obligation specifically to burn. So too wrote the Arukh Ha-shulḥan 294:3. And the Ḥatam Sofer (OḤ 180) wrote that if one burns them he fulfills a mitzva, but there is no obligation in this, and therefore we do not find that our rabbis were particular about it.

There are three stages in the growth of the fruit: 1) Semadar – it is not yet considered a fruit; this is from the time the blossom falls and the tiny fruit is revealed until it reaches the stage at which its shape as a fruit is recognizable. 2) Boser – a fruit not fit for eating; that is, from the time its shape is recognizable it is considered a fruit even though it is not fit for eating. 3) 'Reached a third' – that is, from the time the fruit becomes fit for eating in a time of need, and from then on it is obligated in tithes. According to Rabbi Yossi the prohibition of orla already applies from the semadar stage, and according to the Sages only from the boser stage (Mishna Orla 1:7; Tiferet Yisrael there). And so it is cited in Berakhot 36b, and it is explained there, based on the Mishna (Shevi'it 4:10), that according to Beit Hillel it is forbidden in the Sabbatical year to cut branches of a vine, an olive tree and a carob tree from the time they have boser fruits on them, which in grapes is from when they form kernels, in olives from when they blossom, and in carobs from when they form chains. So too the Radbaz (Responsa 1:44) explained the opinion of the Rambam (Hilkhot Neta Revai 9:13). And so wrote the Gra 294:37. And though regarding unripe dates (kafniyot) they forbade even semadar, this is because people used to eat them (Radbaz). And indeed, in Berakhot 36b they said that regarding other fruits the Sages agree with Rabbi Yossi that semadar too is forbidden, and on this basis the Ḥazon Ish (Orla 3:5) wrote that indeed in other fruits semadar is forbidden, and only in grapes, olives and carobs is semadar permitted and boser forbidden. However, the Gra explained that the words of the Gemara in Berakhot were said as a rebuttal, but the conclusion is that in all fruits semadar is permitted and boser forbidden. And so is the halakha, for it is not reasonable to distinguish between the different types of fruits.
[For those who wish to delve deeper: In SA 294:4 he wrote that at the end of the third year, the fruits that budded (ḥanta) after Tu Bi-Shvat are permitted. And Maran Ha-rav [Kook] in Mishpat Kohen 3 inclined toward this. As is known, according to the Rambam, the Shulḥan Arukh and most poskim, the stage of ḥanata is the stage at which the fruit has reached a third, is fit for eating in a time of need and becomes obligated in tithes (Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it 3, n. 6). But this is difficult for the Shulḥan Arukh, for here we learned that boser fruits are forbidden as orla, and how could it be that when Tu Bi-Shvat arrives they would become permitted? And indeed, the language of the Rambam (Hilkhot Neta Revai 9:10) is: "Everything the tree puts forth within this time is orla," and it is implied that his intention is from when it puts forth – from when it reaches the boser stage. And according to Tosafot, ḥanata is from the time of semadar, and it is possible that Rashi, who wrote (Rosh Hashana 14a) that in the years of orla one follows the ḥanata, intended the opinion of Tosafot. So too wrote Mishpetei Eretz 2:2, that one follows the ḥanata according to Tosafot. However, one can explain that according to the Shulḥan Arukh, from the 1st of Tishrei until Tu Bi-Shvat of the last year, the prohibition of orla is only because the fruits grew by the power of the previous year's rains, and it is reasonable that only fruits that budded before Tu Bi-Shvat grew on the previous year's rains, but those that reached only boser already grew on the rains of the new year and there is no prohibition in them. And it is possible that the Rambam too, who did not explain his opinion, agrees with this.]

sections.body_en:
In counting the years of orla we take into account two dates: the 1st of Tishrei, which is the New Year for years and for plantings, and Tu Bi-Shvat (the 15th of Shevat), which is the New Year for trees; this is because any fruit that buds by Tu Bi-Shvat certainly budded by the power of the rains that the tree received in the previous year. We have another rule: thirty days in a year are considered a year (Rosh Hashana 9b-10b).

This is the calculation: If the tree took root in the ground by the 29th of Av, then by the 1st of Tishrei thirty days will have passed for it, and those thirty days will be counted for it as a full year. Afterward one must wait another two years until the completion of the three years, and since the New Year for trees is Tu Bi-Shvat, one must wait until Tu Bi-Shvat, for the fruits that bud before Tu Bi-Shvat budded by the power of the previous year's rains, when the tree was still orla. Thus, if the tree took root on the 29th of Av 5781, all the fruits that bud on it until Tu Bi-Shvat of the year 5784 will be orla. And all that bud on it from Tu Bi-Shvat 5784 until Tu Bi-Shvat 5785 will be neta revai (fourth-year fruit), and all the fruits that bud on it from Tu Bi-Shvat 5785 will be ḥullin (ordinary, unsanctified). Thus, in practice the law of orla will apply to it for two years and five and a half months.

The Sages estimated that after fourteen days the seed or the cutting takes root in the ground. It emerges that in order for the tree to take root in the ground by the 29th of Av and gain a year, one must plant it at the latest on the 15th of Av. And if one planted a seedling with its clod of earth, there is no need to wait fourteen days, for from the time it is placed in the ground it is considered rooted in it. Consequently, if it is placed in the ground by the 29th of Av, a year is gained.

But if the tree took root in the ground from the 30th of Av 5781 onward, since it did not have thirty days in the year 5781, one begins to count the first year for it only on the 1st of Tishrei 5782, and one will need to wait three full years until the 1st of Tishrei 5785; and since the New Year for trees is Tu Bi-Shvat, one will need to wait several more months for it until Tu Bi-Shvat 5785, and only then will the law of orla depart from the tree. Thus, if the tree took root in the ground on the 30th of Av 5781, the law of orla applies to it for three years and five and a half months. And indeed, there are lenient authorities who hold that the law of orla never lasts more than three years; however, since the law of orla is by Torah law, the halakha follows the stringent opinion.5

[Video]

notes_en.en:
Took root on the 29th of Av – the years of orla will end after about two and a half years:
[Diagram: Took root on the 29th of Av – the years of orla will end after about two and a half years]
Took root on the 30th of Av – the years of orla will end after three and a half years:
[Diagram]
I wrote according to the opinion of the Razah, Tosafot, Rashba, Ritva, Ran and Tur, that always after the completion of the three years of orla, one must wait until Tu Bi-Shvat, for the fruits that bud until Tu Bi-Shvat draw their vitality from the previous year's rains. However, the first year need not be complete, and if it had thirty days before the 1st of Tishrei, they are considered one year. However, according to Rashi, the Rambam and the Ra'avad (Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni Ve-neta Revai 9:10-12), the Rid, the Meiri and the Semag, only a tree for which we were lenient at its beginning, counting part of the year as a year, must wait until Tu Bi-Shvat; but a tree that was planted less than thirty days before the end of the year waits until the 1st of Tishrei 5782 and then begins to count three full years, and on the 1st of Tishrei 5785 the law of orla departs from it, for since three full years have passed over it, it has left the category of orla entirely, and even what buds before Tu Bi-Shvat, which grew by the power of the previous year's rains when it was still orla, is not forbidden. And if one planted the tree between the 1st of Tishrei and Tu Bi-Shvat, according to many following this approach, the three years of orla end on Tu Bi-Shvat, so that one waits more than three full years (Ra'avad, Radbaz and those who agree with them, in explaining the Rambam). And some say that one counts three years from day to day (Kesef Mishneh, in explaining the Rambam). And some say that whether one planted before Rosh Hashana or after it, one never counts more than three years from day to day (Rav Hai Gaon as cited in the Eshkol, Hilkhot Orla 111a; and Rav Natronai Gaon as cited in Tamim De'im 130). And some are even more lenient, that if it took root by the 29th of Av 5781, the years of orla end on the 1st of Tishrei 5784, 25 months after taking root; and if it took root after the 29th of Av, the years of orla end on Tu Bi-Shvat 5784, 29.5 months after taking root (Rabbeinu Ḥananel, Rosh Hashana 9b-10a; some opinions in the Eshkol, Orla 111a).
In practice, as the primary opinion, the Shulḥan Arukh 294:4-5 ruled like the Rambam, and only as 'some say' did he write like the Razah. The Gra also ruled like the Rambam. However, I wrote according to the stringent opinion, for a doubt regarding a Torah law is resolved stringently. So too wrote Rabbi Eliyahu of Fulda, the Levush, Sha'arei Tzedek, and the Aderet. And Rabbi Shlomo Sirilio and Kerem Tziyon vol. 6, 5:5, wrote that it is fitting to be stringent.
Outside the Land the halakha follows the lenient opinion, and in a time of need even the opinion of Rabbeinu Ḥananel. Regarding the fourteen days required for the planting to take root, the intention is full days, and therefore in order for a year to be counted for it, one must plant at the latest on the 15th of Av. So too wrote the Rambam (Hilkhot Neta Revai 9:10), Semag, Kaftor Va-feraḥ, Tur and SA 294:4, Sha'arei Tzedek and the Arukh Ha-shulḥan. And some say that part of the day is like the whole of it, and one may plant on the 16th of Av (Rabbeinu Yeruḥam and Meiri). In the Land of Israel one must be stringent, and outside the Land one may be lenient.

sections.title_en: A Tree That Was Uprooted or Cut Down
sections.body_en:
A tree that was uprooted from its place, if it still has one root left that connects it to the ground, and its thickness is at least that of the needle with which weavers would stretch the garment, may be reburied in the ground and it is exempt from orla, since it can survive with difficulty through this root. And if not even such a root remains, when it is buried in the ground it becomes obligated in orla again (SA 294:20).

A tree that was uprooted by the wind or swept away by a river, and a clod of earth remained attached to its roots: even though it has no root at all connecting it to the ground, if the tree can live for fourteen days from the clod of earth attached to its roots, it may be reburied in the ground and there is no need to count years of orla for it again. And if it cannot live from it for fourteen days, when it is buried in the ground one will need to count the years of orla for it anew. Therefore, when there is a need to move a fruit tree from place to place, one must be careful to uproot it with a clod of earth in which it can live for fourteen days, and in this way one will not need to count years of orla for it from the beginning. And it is good to prune it beforehand as much as possible, for in this way it survives easily for a long time.6

A tree that was cut down or broken, if any amount of its trunk remains above the ground, it is exempt from orla; and if it was cut down entirely and grew again from its root, it is obligated in orla.7

[Video]

notes_en.en: Mishna Orla 1:3: "A tree that was uprooted and the rock (soil) with it… if it can live – it is exempt, and if not – it is obligated." So too wrote the SA 294:19. Some say that only if it can live in its clod for three years is it exempt from orla. So too wrote the Peraḥ Mateh Aharon 2:75; Birkei Yosef 294:11; Pitḥei Teshuva 13; Igrot Moshe YD 1:185. However, the rabbis of the Land, headed by Maran Ha-rav Kook in Mishpat Kohen 8-9, ruled for farmers in practice that it suffices that the tree be able to survive for fourteen days, like the length of the days of taking root. And Rav Herzog, Pesakim U-khtavim 3:9, accepted their opinion. And so ruled Mishpetei Uziel 1:20 and Minḥat Shlomo 1:69. And the intention is that the tree be able to survive in its clod by being given the necessary care of irrigation and fertilizing. And in my humble opinion, even the stringent authorities can agree to this, for if the clod is able to sustain the plant with routine care for fourteen days, presumably it can also sustain it for three years, especially if it is pruned deeply and irrigated continuously with drippers.

It is explained in the Yerushalmi, Shevi'it 1:6, that according to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, whatever was cut down to less than a tefaḥ is obligated in orla, and according to the Sages, if any amount remains above the ground it is exempt from orla, and only if it was cut down entirely is it obligated in orla. According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Neta Revai 10:13), the Rashba, Rabbeinu Yeruḥam and SA 294:18, the halakha follows the Sages. And the Rosh ruled like Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov. And see the Beit Yosef and Shakh 294:31 on the basis of their dispute. In practice the halakha follows the lenient authorities, since it is explained in the Yerushalmi that the basis for obligating a cut-down tree in orla is rabbinic, because of mar'it ayin (appearances), and a doubt regarding a rabbinic law is resolved leniently. Furthermore, this is the opinion of most poskim.

sections.title_en: Havrakha (Layering) and the Law of Suckers
sections.body_en:
To create a 'havrakha' (layering), one bends a branch of a developed tree and buries its middle in the ground, and its tip emerges at the place where one wishes to create an additional tree. At first the havrakha tree draws its vitality from the original tree, and over time the part buried in the ground develops roots, and they too nourish the new tree. Regarding orla, as long as the new tree draws vitality from the original tree, even if most of its vitality comes from the roots of the havrakha, it is drawn after the original tree and is exempt from orla. And even if from the second tree they layered a third tree, and from the third they layered a fourth tree, as long as they are connected to the first tree they are exempt from orla, for they are still considered its continuation. But if the branch connecting the original tree to the havrakha was cut, or this part withered, the havrakha becomes obligated in orla and one must begin to count three years for it.

If new suckers (sorim) came up from under the ground, even though they came up from the root system of the old tree, as long as this is not recognizable, for example where they emerged at a significant distance from the tree, they have the law of a new tree that is obligated in orla (Bava Metzia 119a; Rambam, Hilkhot Neta Revai 10:19). However, if the suckers grew close to the old tree, so that it is recognizable that they are part of it and emerged from its trunk below the ground, there is room to say that according to halakha they do not have the law of orla, since they are part of the old tree. However, since many are stringent in this, considering these suckers too as a new tree, it is proper to be stringent.8

[Video]

notes_en.en: The Chief Rabbinate and the various kashrut bodies customarily rule that suckers that emerged from under the ground (sorim) have the law of a new tree and are obligated in orla, as explained in Bava Metzia 119a; Rambam, Hilkhot Neta Revai 10:19: "A tree that comes out of the trunk – is exempt from orla; from the roots – is obligated in orla." And they rule so even when these suckers are close and adjacent to the main trunk. According to this, one must be careful with pomegranate trees, blueberries and the like, which customarily put out suckers that produce many fruits before the years of orla have passed over them. In practice this is a constant struggle against these suckers, and many stumble in this. However, it appears that according to the basic law there is no prohibition in suckers close to the old trees. For the tree is its root system and the beginning of its trunk, and as long as additional branches grow from this system there is no prohibition of orla in them, as we learned regarding the caper, which sometimes withers entirely in winter and grows again from its roots, and its law is like a tree which, after three years, is exempt from orla (as explained in the Shibbolei Ha-leket 160, in the name of Rabbeinu Ḥananel; and see below, note 11). It emerges, then, that everything explained in the Rambam and the poskim as forbidden concerns suckers that emerge far from the trunk and come up from the lateral roots and not from the center of growth of the tree. And something similar was written by my teacher Rav Yisraeli (Amud Ha-yemini 28) and the Minḥat Shlomo (vol. 1, 71:8). And so it is implied according to what the Rashba wrote, that the entire prohibition of suckers is rabbinic because of mar'it ayin, and so too wrote the Rash of Sens and the Keren Ora. And in suckers close to the trunk there is no concern of mar'it ayin, for it is recognizable that they are part of the main tree. And if this were not so, it is very difficult to understand why many did not mention the ruling of the Rambam at all, among them the Tur and the Shulḥan Arukh; and even those who mentioned the words of the Rambam did not properly detail this severe and common prohibition in which many pomegranate growers stumble. Rather, one is compelled to say that there is no prohibition in this. In addition, according to the Or Zarua, based on his version of the Gemara (Bava Metzia 119a), all suckers that emerge from the roots are exempt from orla (like the law of havrakha), and in a rabbinic matter it is possible that one may rely on him. However, since many customarily rule today that these suckers are forbidden, and some even fear that the prohibition is by Torah law, it is proper to take their approach into account (Mishpetei Eretz 6:4; and see the article of Rav Yoel Friedman, Emunat Itekha 14).

sections.body_en:
A tree growing inside a house is obligated in orla, for the main thing regarding the obligation of orla is that the tree be planted in the ground, and the roof above it does not exempt it from orla. Likewise, a tree planted on the roof of a house is obligated in orla; and although air separates the roof from the ground, since the roof itself is connected to the ground through the walls, the roof itself is considered part of the ground and the tree upon it is considered as planted in the ground (SA 294:26).

One who plants a seedling in a perforated pot is considered as planting in the ground, and begins to count the years of orla. Likewise, one who plants a tree in an unperforated earthenware pot – the tree is considered as planted in the ground and is obligated in orla, for since its roots can break through the earthenware, even before they break through it they are considered as drawing from the ground. And some say that even a tree growing in a metal pot is obligated in orla, even though it is clear that the roots cannot penetrate it.9

Following the development of agriculture, with the improvement of fertilizing and irrigation, many trees are able to yield many fruits in the third year. And since the fruits are forbidden for benefit, and there is a loss in the trees occupying expensive land for nothing, a solution was found for this: to keep the trees for about two years in nurseries inside perforated plastic pots, where they occupy a small space and the cost of maintaining them is low, and in the third year to transfer them to the ground, so that they will strengthen in the soil and yield many fruits in the fourth year, whose fruits are permitted.

In practice, since one takes into account the opinion of those who hold that an unperforated plastic pot is exempt from orla, in order that the time the plantings spend in the pots be counted toward the three years of orla according to all opinions, one must be careful about two things: 1) That there be in the pot a hole the size of a small root, by means of which it will be considered connected to the ground; and it is customary to be stringent that the hole be 2.5 cm in diameter.10 2) When transferring the seedling from the pot to the ground, the clod around the roots must not fall apart. After the fact, even if most of it fell apart, as long as its roots have a clod of earth in which they are rooted, it can still survive by means of it, and there is no need to count three years for it again. But if almost the entire clod fell apart, to the point that there is concern that without placing it in the ground, even with irrigating and tending the clod, it could not survive for 14 days, one must count three years of orla for it from the beginning.11

notes_en.en: According to the Rosh (Responsa, Kelal 2:4) and the Tur (as explained in Ḥavat Binyamin 2:4 and Minḥat Shlomo 1:70, p. 400), only what grows in an unperforated earthenware pot is obligated in orla, and what grows in other unperforated pots, including a wooden pot, is exempt from orla; consequently, when the seedling is transferred to the ground, one must begin to count three years for it. However, the Rambam (Hilkhot Neta Revai 10:8) wrote: "One who plants in an unperforated pot – is obligated in orla; although it is not like the ground for seeds, it is like the ground for trees." So too wrote SA 294:26. And this is the opinion of most poskim. However, they disagree about which pots are meant. Some say specifically a wooden pot and the like, which in certain cases the roots of the tree can break through, but pots that the roots cannot break through are entirely exempt from orla (Rav Herzog, Pesakim U-khtavim vol. 3, 10). And some say that in any pot whatsoever, even one of iron, the trees are obligated in orla, because the roots of a tree are considered so large and strong that no partition is considered to interrupt their drawing from the ground (Minḥat Shlomo vol. 3, 158:20). And some were in doubt about this (Har Tzvi, Zera'im vol. 2, 15:3; Le-horot Natan 6:101). And since the doubt concerns a Torah prohibition, one must be stringent with an unperforated iron or wooden pot: on the one hand, the seedling in it is obligated in orla, and on the other hand, if it was afterward transferred to the ground, one begins to count three years anew.

Generally the plantings are grown in a plastic bag that has a hole in it; but if it is thick and has no hole at all, the roots of a small tree will not break through it. And then, according to the Rosh, the tree growing there is exempt from orla and one does not begin to count three years for it; and some hold that this is the law according to the Rambam and those who agree with him as well, as we learned in the previous note. Therefore one must make a hole in the bag, by means of which the planting will be considered connected to the ground and will become obligated in orla, and consequently one will begin to count the three years for it. The size of the hole we learned from other laws: it is the size of a small root (Uktzin 2:10), and in the Gemara (Shabbat 95b) we learned that it is larger than a hole through which liquid enters (which is less than 2 mm), and smaller than the width of an olive (which is about 1.5 cm in our ordinary olive). In practice it became customary to be very stringent in this and to equate the size of a small root with the size of a kezayit, which is larger than our olive, and thus it came about that a hole of 2.5 cm is required (Rav Goren, Teḥumin 1, p. 158; Mishpetei Eretz 3:7, n. 1). However, after the fact, in my humble opinion even a hole of one centimeter can suffice, since it is more than the size of a small root. In addition, according to the Rambam even an unperforated pot is obligated in orla. And although some hold according to his opinion that a wooden pot that the roots are unable to break through is exempt, it is possible that they do break through a plastic bag, and then according to most poskim it turns out that there is no need for a hole at all (so too wrote Rav Goren there). Moreover, even when there is a small hole of a millimeter there, since it is a bag, the root that passes there is able to widen it to more than the size of a kezayit, and consequently it is reasonable that its law is like that of an earthenware pot, which even according to the Rosh is considered perforated. In addition, some hold that even a tree growing in a completely unperforated pot, which is exempt from orla, has three years counted for it, just as years are counted for a planting brought from outside the Land (Beit David vol. 2, 1; Even Ha-azel as cited in Kerem Tziyon). And see the extensive article of my friend Rav Azriel Ariel, shlita, in Ha-Torah Ve-ha'aretz vol. 1.

When the seedlings are transported from the nursery to the field, they are in a truck that has a metal floor, and some were concerned lest they be considered during that time as detached from the soil, so that when they are planted again in the ground, one would need to count three years for them again; and therefore they required, ideally, transporting them in a truck whose floor is perforated (Rav Ovadia Yosef; Shevet Ha-levi 5:156:3-4). However, according to the law there is no need for this, since the seedling remains with its clod in such a way that it survives through it without any change, and after an interruption of several hours it is not considered as being replanted (Rav Yisraeli in Ḥavat Binyamin 1:1; Minḥat Shlomo vol. 3, 158:19; 1:70; Mishpetei Eretz 3:9, n. 7). And this is in addition to those who hold, according to the Rambam and most poskim, that even a seedling in a metal pot is obligated in orla, and in addition to the opinion of the Beit David mentioned at the end of the previous note. And see the above-mentioned article of Rav Azriel.

sections.title_en: Defining the Trees Obligated in Orla
sections.body_en:
The mitzva of orla applies to fruit trees and not to vegetables, and even vegetables that grow on perennial bushes are exempt from orla. The main difference between a tree and a perennial vegetable is that the stem of a perennial vegetable withers each year and grows again the next year from its roots, whereas the trunk of a tree, with its roots, remains and grows stronger from year to year, and from it branches and fruits continue to grow each year. According to this the blessing over eating the fruit is also determined, 'Ha-etz' or 'Ha-adama'. Therefore one recites 'Ha-adama' over a banana; and although it grows to a height of about four meters and looks like a tree, since each year its trunk withers and its roots wilt and it grows again from its bulb, it is considered a vegetable (Berakhot 40a; following the Ge'onim; SA and Rema OḤ 203:2-3; Peninei Halakha, Berakhot 8:2).12

Regarding eggplants and peppers a question arose, since their stem remains from year to year. However, in practice they do not have the law of orla, for they are entirely different from a tree: they give fruit already in the first year, and in the second year their fruits diminish in quantity and quality, and they do not give fruit for more than three years. And as we learned in the Torah, a tree gives fruit for at least five years, and in the merit of keeping the mitzva of orla its fruits increase and improve in the fifth year, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:23-25): "And when you come into the land and plant any tree for food, you shall treat its fruit as forbidden; three years it shall be forbidden to you, it shall not be eaten. And in the fourth year all its fruit shall be holy, for giving praise to the Lord. And in the fifth year you may eat its fruit, so that it may increase its yield for you; I am the Lord your God." And as the Sages said: "This mitzva that you keep will serve to increase its yield for you, for as its reward I will bless for you the fruits of the planting. Rabbi Akiva used to say: The Torah spoke in response to the evil inclination, so that a person should not say, 'Behold, for four years I trouble myself over it for nothing'; therefore it is stated: 'so that it may increase its yield for you; I am the Lord' – I am the Lord who promises this and am faithful to keep My promise" (Rashi, based on Torat Kohanim there). And so the Ramban explains (there), that the fruits growing in the third year are few and poor, and only in the fourth year do they become good and fit to be brought before God, as in the mitzva of neta revai.

Accordingly, there is also no law of orla in papaya and passion fruit, since they give fruit already in the first year, and by the fifth year their fruits diminish, and many of them also do not survive for five years. True, some are stringent in this, but the main view follows those who permit. Likewise, there is no law of orla in raspberries and blackberries [?] of all their kinds, as explained in the note.13

notes_en.en: Tosefta Kilayim (3:15): "This is the rule: whatever puts forth its leaves from its root is a vegetable, and whatever does not put forth its leaves from its root is a tree." That is, a vegetable each year puts forth its leaves from its base, which is its root or its bulb, whereas a tree has a trunk and roots that grow stronger from year to year, and from the trunk the leaves come out each year. And regarding the blessing of 'Ha-adama' or 'Ha-etz', they said in Berakhot 40b: "Wherever, when you take the fruit, there is no gavza (stock) remaining that again produces [fruit] – we do not recite over it 'Borei Peri Ha-etz' but 'Borei Peri Ha-adama'." Some explained that the Rishonim disagreed about the definition of 'gavza' and consequently about the definition of a tree. According to their explanation, according to the Rosh a tree is anything whose roots remain from year to year; according to the Ge'onim it is a tree only if the trunk above the ground remains from year to year; and some understood from Rashi that it is a tree only if the branches too remain from year to year. And from this many doubts arose regarding blessings and orla. And it seems more likely in my humble opinion that the Rishonim did not intend to disagree; rather, all agree that a tree is a plant that has a trunk and roots that endure and grow stronger from year to year, and by virtue of this their fruits increase from year to year, as we shall learn in the next note. However, Rashi described the common tree, whose branches too endure from year to year, and the Ge'onim were precise to include in their definition also trees whose branches wither, and the Rosh was even precise to say that sometimes the trunk above the ground also withers, as sometimes happens with the caper; and nevertheless, since it has a single system of trunk and roots that grows stronger from year to year, it is a tree, as was decided in the Gemara (Berakhot 36a). And this definition of a tree fits all the talmudic discussions, and according to it the raspberry is not a tree, as explained in the next note.

The poskim dealt extensively with the law of eggplants, whose stem endures into the second year, and seemingly according to this they have the law of orla; and so wrote the Kaftor Va-feraḥ (chapter 56). However, everyone customarily eats them, and the Birkei Yosef 294:4 wrote in the name of his grandfather Rabbi Avraham Azulai that so too was the practice of the righteous who were accustomed to be stringent with themselves, among them Rabbi Yosef Karo, the Arizal and Rabbi Moshe Alsheikh: "Because every tree that produces fruit every year keeps improving, whereas this tree of the badinjan (eggplant) in the first year is good and sweet, and in the second year it declines a little and is somewhat bitter, and in the third year it is very bitter, such that it is not fit for eating except under duress; and this indicates that it is a vegetable." So too wrote Mishpetei Uziel 6:80. And some further wrote that it cannot be that there would be a fruit forbidden to eat forever (Penei Moshe YD 294:4; Igrot Ha-re'aya 468; Ḥazon Ish, Orla 12:3).
In practice, the poskim wrote various signs for defining a bush that is exempt from orla. Many wrote that whatever gives fruit in its first year is not a tree (Radbaz 3:531; Kol Eliyahu; Ma'amar Mordekhai; Peri Adama; Rav Pe'alim vol. 2, OḤ 30). Some wrote that if its trunk is hollow – it is not a tree but a stalk, even if it is thick, for only a stalk-trunk can grow quickly, whereas a woody trunk grows over several years (Halakhot Ketanot 1:83; Rav Pe'alim there). And some wrote, as cited above, that its fruits become poor from year to year (Birkei Yosef; Tzitz Eliezer 2:15).
According to these signs, there is no law of orla in papaya and passion fruit. True, in Mishpetei Eretz 1:4 he was stringent regarding papaya because it gives fruit for more than three years. And some added the argument that sometimes it survives even ten years or more. And Rav Yoel Friedman was stringent regarding passion fruit (Emunat Itekha 26), because there is no significant decline in the quantity of its fruits, and its trunk is not truly hollow; furthermore, if it is pruned well the fruits will not diminish during the three years. However, from the standpoint of halakha, many poskim ruled that whatever gives fruit in the first year is not a tree, and papaya and passion fruit give fruit in the first year. And so ruled in practice regarding papaya the Rav Pe'alim (vol. 2, OḤ 30), Yayin Ha-tov vol. 1, YD 14; Rav Eliyahu (Ma'amar Mordekhai 3:10); Yeḥaveh Da'at 4:52. In addition, the papaya trunk is hollow, and in the passion fruit trunk too there is a small hollow (Responsa Ḥelkat Ha-sadeh 1:16-17). Likewise, from the standpoint of essence, a tree is a plant that grows for the long term, and its fruits increase in the fifth and sixth years and it continues to give a yield for many years. Whereas the papaya does not grow on average more than five years and its fruits diminish from year to year. And likewise with passion fruit, the peak yield is in the first and second years, and perhaps also the third, and afterward the yield keeps declining, and naturally many of the bushes wither by the fifth year.
Raspberry looks like a bush that endures many years, but in truth a branch comes out of the ground that gives fruit in the first two years, or only in the second year, and afterward it withers. Meanwhile new branches come out of the ground, and they too give fruit for about two years and wither. And there is also some hollowness in the raspberry stem. In practice, since each stem gives fruit for two years at most, the law of the raspberry is like a vegetable and its blessing is 'Ha-adama'. And so is the law of blackberries [?] and all bushes whose branches wither in the third year. True, sometimes the new raspberry branch grows out of the old stem, and it is possible that it even draws a little from it; but in truth the new one does not need the old one, and those attached to the old stem do not grow more than those that grow anew from the roots. Thus even those attached to the stem grow for themselves a nourishing system suited to their growth, and there is no tree here that keeps growing stronger from year to year.

sections.title_en: One Who Plants Not for the Sake of Fruit
sections.body_en:
One who plants a fruit tree not for the sake of its fruit but for the sake of its timber or so that it will serve as a fence – the fruits growing on it do not have the law of orla, since it is not considered a food tree, whereas the mitzva of orla applies only to a food tree, as it is stated (Vayikra 19:23): "and plant any tree for food – you shall treat its fruit as forbidden." However, the Sages said that one may be lenient in this on condition that it is recognizable that the tree is planted there not for the sake of eating its fruit; for example, the trees are very dense, so that it is recognizable that they were planted in order to use their wood for burning; or one prunes its branches in a way that causes them to thicken, so that it is recognizable that the tree was planted in order to use its branches as planks for building; or by the precise location of the trees' planting it is recognizable that they were planted to serve as a fence for the courtyard. And even if one intended that only one side of the tree would serve as a fence while its other side would be for growing fruit, the fence side is exempt from orla and the fruit side is obligated in orla (Mishna and Yerushalmi, Orla 1:1; SA 294:23). And if he wishes to eat the permitted fruits, he should separate terumot and ma'asrot from them without a blessing (see Yerushalmi Orla 1:1). And if he planted the tree both for a fence or timber and for fruit, its fruits have the law of orla.

Those who plant trees for ornament, such as olive trees, the fruits do not have the law of orla. However, a doubt arose regarding trees that were planted for ornament, but where the beauty of their fruits is also desired, such as pomegranates and date palms. And since the law of orla is by Torah law, one must be stringent in the doubt. Only when it is clear that they did not intend the beauty of the fruits do they not have the law of orla.

The fruits growing on the trees in the fourth year are holy, and it is a mitzva to eat them in purity in Jerusalem, like the law of ma'aser sheni (below 7:9-10). If he wishes, the owner of the fruits may redeem the fruits with money, bring the money up to Jerusalem, buy food with it and eat it in purity. Since the fruits of neta revai are holy, there is no mitzva to leave from them leket, shikheḥa and pe'a for the poor, and there is no mitzva to separate terumot and ma'asrot from them (Mishna and Yerushalmi, Ma'aser Sheni 5:3-4; Rambam, Hilkhot Neta Revai 9:1-4).

Nowadays, when we cannot bring the fruits of the fourth year up to Jerusalem and eat them in purity, we redeem all the fruits with money or something of monetary value, and thereby permit the fruits to be eaten. And although they are many fruits, since we are forbidden to eat them nowadays, they have no value at all; but it is impossible to perform an act of redemption with less than the value of a peruta, and therefore one redeems all the fruits onto a coin worth at least a peruta or onto a food worth a peruta. Before the redemption one recites: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning the redemption of revai," and says: "All these fruits are redeemed with this peruta," or "with this food that is worth a peruta." And the peruta or the food that became sanctified through the redemption is destroyed, so that people will not stumble and benefit from it (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 10:16-17). All the details of these laws will be explained below in the laws of the redemption of ma'aser sheni (below 10:6-8).14

The laws of orla and neta revai also apply to the fruits of the Sabbatical year: if the fruits are in the first three years of the tree – they are orla and forbidden to eat; and if they are in the fourth year – anyone is permitted to pick them, but they must be eaten in Jerusalem, and nowadays they must be deconsecrated onto a peruta. Owners of fields must mark the trees in the Sabbatical year, so that those who come to the field will be careful with them when they are orla, and will know to redeem them when they are neta revai. After their redemption one must be careful to finish eating them by the time of bi'ur (removal), and if one did not do so, one must remove them in the way that the other fruits of the Sabbatical year must be removed (Rambam, Hilkhot Neta Revai 9:7; Peninei Halakha, Shevi'it 4:5).

The poskim disagree regarding 'neta revai' outside the Land. Some say that since it is a halakha le-Moshe mi-Sinai that the mitzva of orla applies outside the Land, the mitzva of neta revai also applies outside the Land, for orla and neta revai depend on each other (Talmidei Rabbeinu Yona, Ri the Elder). And some say that the law of neta revai is like the law of ma'aser sheni, which applies only in the Land of Israel (Rambam). Ideally it is good to fulfill all opinions and to redeem neta revai outside the Land without a blessing (Shakh 294:17). And one who wishes to be lenient and not redeem – may do so, for just as one is lenient in doubtful orla outside the Land, so the halakha follows the lenient opinion in doubtful neta revai.15

notes_en.en:
The poskim disagree regarding a person who redeems his own fruits. Some say that he must add a fifth, as with ma'aser sheni (Mishpetei Eretz 12:6). And some say that there is no need to add a fifth, for the law of the fifth was not stated in the Torah regarding neta revai, and consequently nowadays one redeems everything with a peruta (Kesef Mishneh, Hilkhot Ma'akhalot Assurot 10:17; SA 294:6). And even for one who wishes to be stringent, some are concerned that if he says "it and its fifth onto a peruta," it will turn out that the fruit itself is redeemed for less than a peruta (Or Le-Tziyon vol. 1, YD 25).
One redeems the fruits of 'revai' only after they have been picked. In a pressing situation, one may redeem them while still attached, conditionally, that is, he says that the redemption will take effect after they are picked, and he should not recite the blessing when he says this, because at that time the redemption has not yet taken effect. And this redemption is effective on condition that the fruits have already reached the stage of obligation in tithes, that is, that it is possible to eat them in a time of need, and the coin must remain until after they are picked.

Some say that 'neta revai' applies outside the Land only in a vineyard and not in other plantings, nor in a vine that is not planted as part of a vineyard (below 4:3). This is because the Tanna'im disagree whether the mitzva of the fourth year applies to all trees or only to a vineyard, and although in the Land of Israel it was ruled that it applies to all trees, outside the Land the halakha follows the lenient opinion, and it applies only to a vineyard (Ge'onim, Rosh, Rema). In practice, ideally it is good to fulfill all opinions and to redeem the fruits of neta revai from all trees outside the Land; however, according to the law, since one is lenient in doubtful orla outside the Land, one may also be lenient regarding a doubtful fourth-year vineyard outside the Land, and all the more so regarding doubtful neta revai.
Some say that just as the law of orla nowadays is by Torah law, so the law of neta revai is by Torah law (Mabit; see Minḥat Shlomo vol. 1, 71:13). And some say that the law of neta revai is like the law of ma'aser sheni, and then, according to the Rambam and those who agree with him, who hold that terumot and ma'asrot nowadays are rabbinic, so too is the law of neta revai (Minḥat Ḥinukh 247:15; Yeshu'ot Malko).
Simply understood, the mitzva of eating the fruits of ma'aser sheni is fulfilled only when the Temple and the altar stand in their place, for the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni 2:1) that ma'aser sheni is not eaten nowadays in Jerusalem, because it is compared to the firstborn animal, which is eaten only when the altar stands in its place (Makkot 19a). And the Rambam wrote (there 9:1) that the law of neta revai is like that of ma'aser sheni, and so too wrote the Gra 294:17.

sections.body_en:
Orla fruits that became mixed with ordinary fruits of the same kind: as long as the kosher fruits are not two hundred times the orla, the entire mixture is forbidden. For so the Sages established: teruma, which is forbidden to eat and permitted for benefit, is nullified in one hundred, whereas orla and kilayim, which are forbidden to eat and for benefit, are nullified in two hundred (Mishna Orla 2:1).

All this is when the orla fruits became mixed in among the permitted fruits. But if a doubt arose regarding certain fruits that a person bought, whether they are orla or not, the law depends on the question of where the doubt arose. If the fruits were bought in the orchard or near the orchard, even though most orchards and trees are not orla, since the tree or the orchard has a fixed place, the orla fruits are not nullified, according to the rule: "Kol kavua ke-meḥtza al meḥtza dami" (anything fixed is considered as half and half), and the fruits are forbidden. But if the fruits were bought after they had been separated from their fixed place and brought to the market or to the stores, then it is an ordinary doubt, and one follows the majority, according to the rule: "Kol de-parish me-ruba parish" (whatever separates is considered as separating from the majority).

However, all this is after the fact, regarding a person who bought fruits and does not know what their status is, or who is in a place where there are no stores with a kashrut certificate and to reach such a store he would have to go to great trouble. But if there is a store there with a kashrut certificate, he must avoid the doubt and buy there. And even if he knows that it is a very remote doubt, because the percentage of orla in these fruits or in this area is extremely low, when possible one is obligated to avoid the doubt. In addition, it is a mitzva to strengthen those who are meticulous about kashrut. Furthermore, when there is a kashrut certificate, terumot and ma'asrot are also separated properly.16

notes_en.en:
If he bought from the orchard, but there is a doubt whether there is an orla orchard in the area, or there is a doubt whether within the orchard that is not orla there are young trees whose fruits are orla: some say that this doubt too is considered a fixed doubt (Ran; and the MB 513:31 inclined to this). And some say that if it is likely that there is orla there, it is a fixed doubt (Petaḥ Ha-devir). And according to most Rishonim and Aḥaronim, when there is a doubt whether there is any prohibition at all, one follows the majority (Rokeaḥ, Ritva, Radbaz, Magen Avraham and Taz).
Moreover, according to most poskim, in order for the doubt to be considered a fixed doubt, the prohibition must be recognizable in its place, and with slight effort one must be able to clarify where the orchard or the orla trees are. And although some are stringent, the halakha follows the lenient authorities, because according to most poskim, when there is a doubt whether the doubt is considered fixed or separated, one is lenient and considers it separated.
When the fruits were brought to the market there are four possibilities: 1) When the Jewish owner of the fruits brought them to the market and he knows whether they are orla, the doubt arose only in the market, and consequently it has the law of 'separated'. 2) When a gentile brought them to the market, it is clear that since they were separated to the market, their law is that of 'separated'. 3) When a secular Jew brought them from the fixed place to sell them to wholesalers and store owners without knowing their status: some say that since he is obligated in the mitzvot, the doubt arose when he took them from the fixed place, and one must be stringent in their doubt, like the law of a fixed doubt (Yad Yehuda; Minḥat Yitzḥak 7:96). And some say that since he is not careful, the doubt arose only with the careful Jew who took from him, and consequently it is an ordinary doubt (Ḥemdat Shlomo; Minḥat Shlomo vol. 1, 71:12). 4) When a secular Jew sent an agent to buy fruits for him from the orchards, and the agent bought without knowing from where: some say that their law is that of a fixed doubt (Divrei Ḥayim vol. 2, YD 53), and some say that their law is that of an ordinary doubt (Rabbi Shlomo Kluger in Tuv Ta'am Va-da'at, Telita'a 2:14). Thus in two situations it is a situation of 'separated', and in two situations it is doubtful whether it is fixed or separated. And we have already learned that in a doubt whether it is considered fixed or separated, one considers it separated, all the more so when most likely that is the situation. And so many ruled regarding fruits in the market, that their law is that of a separated doubt, and it is permitted to eat them (Minḥat Yitzḥak 7:96; Minḥat Shlomo 1:71:12; Yabi'a Omer 6, YD 24; and others).
However, all this is for a situation after the fact, when one already bought from a store fruits regarding which there is a doubt whether they are orla. But ideally one is obligated to go to trouble to avoid the doubt, and when there is a store in the vicinity that is known not to sell orla, one is obligated to buy from it (Rav Eliyahu wrote similarly in 'Ha-Torah Ve-ha'aretz' vol. 1). And so has the Chief Rabbinate conducted itself since the days of Rav Goren, supervising the orchards so that they do not market orla fruits to the markets under their supervision, and all the stores supervised today by the batei din rely on the supervision system of the Chief Rabbinate. And how much trouble must one go to in order to buy from a supervised store that does not sell orla? In my humble opinion, one can learn from the laws of washing hands and of a minyan, that one must go to the trouble of up to the distance of walking a mil (about a kilometer) (see Peninei Halakha, Tefilla 2:4).
Rav Elyashiv has a complex opinion: as long as there is a likelihood that the fruits are from an orla orchard – that is, if orla fruits are about five percent of all the fruits in the Land, it is likely that in every region of the Land there is also an orla orchard – even after they separated from the orchards and reached the market, in his opinion they have the law of a rabbinic 'fixed' status, for according to some of the poskim (Rosh, Ri and Shakh), the Sages decreed regarding a rabbinic 'fixed' situation that whatever separates from it is forbidden, lest one take from the fixed place. And his opinion is explained at length in Mishpetei Eretz vol. 2, Orla 14. However, since in every doubt concerning the law of 'fixed' the halakha follows the lenient authorities, all the more so regarding a rabbinic 'fixed' situation, one need not be concerned for his approach, in accordance with the words of the other poskim mentioned.
